title: Lockbox SLA & Isolation Playbook — Procurement Scripts and Competitive Notes
content:
TL;DR:

We need a concise, procurement-ready narrative that frames Redwood Dedicated as a 'lockbox' for inference: predictable throughput + operational isolation + contractable SLAs that shift execution risk off the buyer. This doc bundles: short messaging for sales, negotiation scripts for procurement/legal, competitive callouts, and a checklist of artifacts to attach to an RFP.

Audience and decision flow (who we are convincing):
- Platform engineering (technical eval; cares about throughput, queueing, burst reliability).
- Infrastructure/ops leads (isolation, noisy-neighbor risk, tenancy controls).
- Procurement & Legal (contract language; credits; termination rights; audit).
- Finance (unit economics, runway / committed spend).
- CISO/compliance (VPC, KMS, logs).

One-line positioning for pitch decks: "Redwood Dedicated = a contract-backed inference lockbox: isolation, throughput SLOs, and fallbacks so your product never stalls."

Core value pillars and plain-language definitions (use these verbatim in briefs):
1) Predictable throughput (SLO-backed): a committed slots model with token throughput guarantees measured per 5m window.
   - What it means: guaranteed average and burst capacity for steady-state and short bursts.
   - Buyer impact: predictable latency and throughput budgets for SLAs to downstream customers.
2) Tenant isolation (soft + hard controls): compute isolation plus tenancy policies and tenancy-reserved resources.
   - What it means: physical or reserved GPU pools; limits on multi-tenant sharing; optional single-tenant racks for PHI/PCI needs.
   - Buyer impact: reduces noisy-neighbor risk and regulatory exposure.
3) Contractable operational SLAs: uptime, tail-latency percentiles, and invocation success targets with credit schedule.
   - What it means: credits tied to measurable metrics and a clear escalation path.
   - Buyer impact: shifts operational risk to Redwood and gives procurement/compliance language to sign.
4) Graceful fallback & runbook support: automated model routing to lower-cost/compatible variants under contention + runbook for failover testing.
   - Buyer impact: keeps customer-facing features live even if primary model or AZ is degraded.

Competitive callouts (short, battle-ready notes):
- AWS-managed endpoints / SageMaker: strength = deep cloud integration + global regions. Weakness = less opinionated inference runtime, opaque latency/cost tradeoffs, and procurement expects cloud T&Cs rather than inference SLAs. Use: stress that Redwood provides inference-native commitments (per-token economics and model-aware fallbacks) vs. generic VM-based SLAs.
- Self-hosted open-source stack (customer-managed): strength = full control and potential lower marginal cost at scale. Weakness = build/ops burden, unclear TCO, hiring ramp. Use: price-in ops burn and the hidden tax of model upgrades + quantization/caching expertise. Offer migration/managed-services add-on as bridge.
- Other LLM APIs / competitors with shared pools: strength = low friction and price. Weakness = noisy neighbor, capacity surprises, no enterprise isolation. Use: emphasize isolation guarantees and predictable commit pricing.

Procurement-ready language snippets (copy-paste friendly):
- SLA summary clause (short): "Redwood Inference will maintain Dedicated Capacity with throughput availability of >= 99.5% measured per calendar month for committed token throughput at the committed configuration. If throughput availability falls below the stated target, Customer will be eligible for Service Credits as described in Appendix A."
- Isolation definition (short): "Dedicated Capacity: compute resources (GPUs and associated runtime) reserved for Customer and not shared with third-party customers. Redwood will ensure tenancy isolation as described in Appendix B; any deviation triggers the Service Credit mechanism."
- Fallback clause (short): "In the event of sustained capacity constraint, Redwood will automatically route requests to pre-agreed compatible model variants or burst capacity within 30 minutes of detection. Customer will be notified and Redwood will remediate within the timeframes in the operational runbook."

Service Credit schedule (proposal; tweak for negotiations):
- 99.0–99.5% => 10% credit of monthly dedicated capacity fee
- 98.0–99.0% => 25% credit
- <98.0% => 50% credit + escalation to exec SLA review
Notes: credits are preferred by procurement but we must guard downside — define clear measurement windows and excluded events (force majeure, customer misuse, scheduled maintenance with notice).

Operational measurement & artifacts to include in an RFP response (attach these):
- Latency/throughput dashboards for representative customers (per-route p50/p95/p99 token latency)
- Historical capacity utilization heatmaps for committed pools
- Test harness / reproducible benchmark script (link to our bench repo) with sample inputs and configs used to generate numbers
- Attack surface & isolation audit summary (network diagrams, tenancy model description)
- Runbook excerpt: failover detection, model routing, escalation contacts
- SOC2 / ISO/PCI blurbs + KMS integration note

Negotiation playbook (field script + anchors):
- Opening anchor: emphasize the value of shifting risk ("we take on the risk of maintaining throughput and isolation"). Ask for 12–18 month commitment as default.
- Concessions ladder: if buyer pushes back on commitment length, offer a ramped pricing schedule (year 1 committed discount smaller, year 2 larger) or a performance-backed pilot: 3-month paid pilot with defined throughput target and conversion credit.
- Pricing anchor language: show committed-per-token price and a defined overage rate (higher than committed to discourage chronic overuse).
- Legal asks to pre-empt: define scheduled maintenance windows, force majeure carveouts, and an audit routine.

Rebuttals to common procurement objections (scripted):
- "This is just another cloud SLA." => "Most cloud SLAs protect hypervisor uptime. Redwood's SLA measures inference throughput and tail latency at the application level and includes model-aware fallbacks — things cloud SLAs don't cover."
- "We can self-host for cheaper." => "Total cost of ownership often neglects ops effort for performance tuning (quantization, kernel selection, batching). We'll share a conservative TCO model showing ops months vs. our managed service. Also offer a hybrid: private deployment + Redwood managed control plane."
- "What if we need to change model?" => "Commitments are to capacity and performance characteristics, not a model binary. We support model swaps as long as the variant meets the agreed performance profile; we perform compatibility validation as part of change control."

Field playbook: what to send to procurement in first touch (email + attachments):
1) Short one-pager (executive summary) — 1 page 
2) Dedicated capacity SLAs (PDF) — 2 pages with measurement definitions
3) Isolation/tenancy whitepaper — 3–4 pages + network diagram
4) Benchmarks & test harness repo link 
5) Runbook excerpt & escalation matrix 
6) Pricing appendix with committed and overage tiers

Open questions / negotiation risks (internal):
- How granular should measurement windows be? We currently measure per-5m windows for throughput; procurement sometimes asks per-second or per-minute for burst-sensitive use cases. Action: confirm engineering feasibility of shorter windows and cost implications. (Owner: Miguel)
- Do we allow credits to be applied off future invoices only (preferred) or cash refunds (procurement asks for refunds sometimes)? Recommend invoice credits. (Owner: Hannah)
- What is the default RTO for fallback routing? We propose 30 minutes detection + auto-route; some customers want <5 minutes. Need SRE confirm. (Owner: Omar)

Example email snippet to procurement (copyable):
"Hi <Name>,

Attached is a one-page summary of Redwood Dedicated Capacity along with our SLA and isolation whitepaper. At a high level, Redwood provides a contract-backed inference lockbox — reserved compute, measurable throughput SLOs, and automated fallbacks to keep your product live under stress. We are happy to walk through measurement details and provide a short, paid pilot to validate performance in your workload.

Best,
Priya (on behalf of Redwood GTM)"

Appendix: Quick competitive scorecard (checklist format for AE to fill in live) — example metrics to capture during buyer calls:
- Is buyer evaluating cloud-managed endpoints, self-hosted, or API-based vendors?
- How sensitive are they to tail latency (p99 target)?
- Regulatory constraints (PHI/PCI/SOC2): yes/no
- Preferred commitment length (0/3/12/24 months)
- Required audit rights / third-party audits

Quick TODOs (who to involve to finalize doc):
- Miguel: confirm measurement granularity and cost of sub-5m windows (due 2026-01-05)
- SRE: produce a default runbook excerpt for inclusion (due 2026-01-12)
- Legal: standard isolation clause + credit schedule template (due 2026-01-20)

Notes to self / drafting voice: keep the language procurement-friendly (short sentences, measurable terms), avoid engineering jargon in SLA paragraphs but include technical appendix for PEM/eng review. This doc should become the default attachment for AE handoffs when customers cross a committed-spend threshold or ask about enterprise isolation.

— end —

Unpolished fragments / brainstorming (leave as-is):
- consider "commitment bands" (bronze/silver/gold) where gold = single-tenant racks + faster SLA credits; silver = reserved pools; bronze = reserved vGPU with shared racks but tenancy-aware scheduling
- possible promo: free 30-day performance discovery + 10% credit on first committed quarter if we miss initial SLO in pilot
- flag: some buyers insist on indemnity for data loss during fallback; probably a no-go, escalate to legal early
